Just a few years ago, before the LLM-assisted-coding-era, I already did not like frameworks as much as I used to.

I liked Rails. But that was more because through Rails I learned the MVC pattern, learned the layer-middelware pattern from Rack (and the ActiveRecord ORM -- but I now no longer like ORMs but that's a different story). Those 2 pattern I still use today in some way or form, and I find them in many modern (Rust) web development frameworks/libs.

So I now no longer use Rails for new projects. These projects were SSR (traditional server-side rendered web apps that use JavaScript sparingly) built with Kotlin+http4k. Http4k is a web library, so no framework there and it feels very good.

The article is very frontend/JS-focussed. I prefer to keep things simpler just use SSR for the UI. This is because above all (1) I dont like JavaScript (not even when my LLM writes it for me) and (2) for the type of application it is not needed to do state management again in the browser (IMHO it's just more code for the same feature).

Sure, a little JS is needed in my apps too. But I (assisted by LLM) use it sparingly and when I use it it's with Alpine.js.

CSS with Tailwind and JS with Alpine makes for pages that are mostly "self contained" (the CSS and JS defined in the same place as the HTML that relates to it), which makes reasoning about them so much easier.

I'd say http4k, Tailwind and Alpine are not frameworks. Maybe Alpine is most framework-like of all of these. At least they are not frameworks in the sense that they do not dictate my project folder structure.

In my latest projects (all LLM assisted) I make heavy use of architecture tests: tests on the shape of my codebase. These tests check that my architecture rules are adhered to. Think of enforcing the MVC pattern; only the pattern that I use is way more split out (instead of M-V-C, it more like: boot - contract - db - domain - filter - handler - job - lib - path - presentation - routing - workflow).

I'd say framework matter more then you are learning something, or when the team needs to have shared code hygiene values, or when you do not use architecture tests yet!
